name: identity-field
intent: Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity.
problem: Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.
context: Applies wherever objects outlive a single operation and are mapped to key-addressed rows: entities behind a Data Mapper or Row Data Gateway, aggregates in a Repository, session caches keyed by table plus id, and object graphs whose children must refer to a parent that is not inserted yet. The key has to survive serialisation and cross-process calls, and for application-generated keys it must exist before the row does.
benefits: Gives objects a storage-backed identity: a Data Mapper, Identity Map or Unit of Work can decide equality by key, so one row is loaded into exactly one instance per session and stale duplicates stop diverging.
Foreign Key Mapping gets a value to write: references travel as keys instead of object graphs, so a child can point at a parent, sibling or aggregate without keeping the other side in memory.
Makes objects addressable outside the process: the key can be put into a URL, session, queue message or cache entry and resolved later, which an object reference cannot do.
Targets writes precisely: UPDATE and DELETE hit exactly one row by key no matter how the business fields changed, so writes neither miss rows nor hit several.

Removes the need for a natural (business) key as the identity: an immutable surrogate keeps object identity stable while names, account numbers or e-mail addresses are corrected, and a single numeric column indexes and joins cheaply.

Enables pre-allocation: with an application-generated key (UUID/ULID) or a range fetched from a sequence or key table, the identity is known before the INSERT, which is what batch writes, idempotent retries and distributed or sharded inserts need.
tradeoffs: Persistence leaks into the domain model: the id member and its unsaved state (null/0) mean nothing in business terms, yet constructors, fixtures, equality and validation must all carry it.

Key origin has an irreducible cost: database-generated keys require a round trip and do not exist before the INSERT, which forces insert ordering for object graphs, blocks batch inserts that need ids and complicates idempotent retries; application-generated keys avoid that but add key size and, for random UUIDs, index and page-locality cost.
Identity is only as stable as the key: changing, reusing or renumbering keys during migrations, imports or merges silently invalidates identity-map entries, caches, foreign keys and stored links.
Sequential surrogate keys leak volume and business metrics and are trivially enumerable - a security and business-intelligence leak unless replaced by UUID/ULID or an opaque external token.

equals/hashCode must follow the identity field, but the key is null until insert: an object put into a set, map or cache before it is persisted changes its hash code afterwards, and keying on mutable business data is worse.

Entities tend to acquire two identities (surrogate key and natural/business key) and the mapping, API and cache layers must agree which one is authoritative; when they disagree, lookups return the wrong instance.
Composite or natural keys push complexity into every mapper and foreign-key mapping, while the surrogate that avoids this costs an extra column and unique index on every table.

participants.responsibility: The entity that carries the identity field; its business state is mutable, its key is not.
The stored primary-key value plus the convention for the state before the row exists (absent/null/0), which only the mapping layer may interpret.
Reads the key from the row when loading, writes the generated key back onto the object after insert, and uses the key to target updates and deletes.
Produces new keys: a database identity/serial column, a sequence, a key table handing out ranges (hi-lo), or an application-side UUID/ULID/snowflake generator.
Keeps one instance per (table, key) in the session, so loading the same key again returns the existing object instead of a second copy.
Declares the primary-key column, its type and its generation strategy and enforces uniqueness; the object only mirrors what the schema owns.

use_cases: ORM entities in a session: load a row into an object, mutate business fields, then flush an UPDATE or DELETE targeted at the same identity.
API resources addressed by key: /orders/{id} endpoints that fetch, mutate and delete by identity, with links stored as keys instead of object references.
Session-scoped identity maps and second-level caches keyed by (table, key), which need the key before they can return an existing instance.
Object graphs with parent-child references: the child's foreign key needs the parent's identity, generated before the insert (UUID/sequence) or read back after it (RETURNING/getGeneratedKeys).
Audit, versioning and optimistic locking: change logs and Version Number checks identify the affected row by its key.
Distributed or sharded writes: client-generated keys let a router place the row and let a retry overwrite the same identity idempotently.

Event-sourced aggregates: the aggregate root's identity is the correlation ID carried in every command and event, allowing the event log to reconstruct state by replaying events keyed to that identity.

GraphQL Relay node identification: globally unique node IDs are built from the entity's identity (base64 type-prefixed id), enabling the standardised node query and cache reching defined in the Relay specification.
Multi-tenant SaaS with tenant-scoped identity: a composite key of (tenant_id, id) ensures a tenant can never address another tenant's rows, even if the local id numbers happen to collide.
Idempotent message processing: a command's correlation ID (the entity's identity) lets a handler detect a duplicate and skip reprocessing without a distributed lock.

Hibernate ORM entities with an @Id and Session persistence context: loading by identifier reuses the session's first-level identity, while the chosen generated-id strategy determines when the key becomes available.
PostgreSQL tables with GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY and INSERT ... RETURNING id: the database owns key generation, then the mapper reads the assigned identity back onto the object in the same write.

Relay GraphQL servers implementing the Node interface: expose a globally unique opaque id and refetch the same object through node(id), carrying entity identity across a client cache and API boundary.
avoid_when: The concept is a value object or immutable data (Embedded Value, Serialized LOB): equality by fields is the point, and an identity field destroys value semantics.
Objects are transient DTOs or read-only projections that are never updated: no mapper has to recognise them, so the key buys nothing.
The store already mints a document key and the whole graph is serialised (Serialized Entity, document stores): adding a second id duplicates identity instead of defining it.
A genuinely immutable, globally unique natural key already exists (ISO country code, ISIN): the surrogate only adds a column, an index and an extra join.
The table is a pure link table (Association Table Mapping) whose composite foreign-key pair is already the identity: a surrogate key hides that uniqueness instead of expressing it.
anti_patterns: Using a mutable business attribute (e-mail, name, account number) as the identity field: correcting that attribute silently changes who the entity is, orphaning identity-map entries, caches and foreign keys.
Spreading the unsaved-state convention through the domain - if (entity.id == null) branches in business logic - instead of keeping 'is new' in the mapper or Unit of Work.
Reusing, renumbering or reassigning keys during migrations, imports or merges while caches, identity maps and stored URLs still hold the old values.
Exposing guessable sequential keys in public URLs or APIs without authorising access to the fetched object: enumeration, scraping and inference of business volume.
Keeping two competing identities (surrogate key and business id) with no rule which one is authoritative, so equals(), caches, resolvers and the mapper disagree about the same entity.
design_principles: Single source of truth: one authoritative key per entity, declared by the schema and only mirrored in the object, never recomputed from business data.
Immutability: the identity field is set once and never mutated; a key change is a delete plus insert, not an update.
Separation of concerns: key generation, key read-back and unsaved-state handling belong to the persistence layer, not to domain behaviour.
Information hiding and referential integrity: references travel as opaque key values, which keeps object graphs small and free of cycles.
Consistency by contract: equals and hashCode follow identity alone, and the key type is used identically from column to API boundary.
best_practices: Choose a meaningless surrogate key (integral identity/sequence, UUID v7, ULID, or Snowflake) instead of a business attribute, and document why.

Decide when the key must be known: generate it in the application (UUID/ULID) or pre-allocate ranges (hi-lo) when it must exist before the INSERT — object graphs, batch writes, queue messages, idempotent retries. Otherwise let the database generate it and read it back in the same statement using RETURNING, getGeneratedKeys(), or OUTPUT INSERTED.
For distributed or multi-tenant systems, use a time-ordered key (UUID v7, ULID, or Snowflake) to preserve B-tree index locality and avoid hot spots.
Never expose sequential integer keys in public URLs or APIs; use UUID/ULID or an opaque external token to prevent enumeration attacks, and always authorise access to the resolved object.

Keep the key type identical end-to-end: column type, in-memory type and wire format. Map 64-bit integers deliberately (e.g., bigint to string in JSON/JavaScript) instead of letting them truncate or lose precision.

Base equals and hashCode on the identity field only; keep entities with an unassigned key out of sets, maps and caches until persisted, or use a stable placeholder (e.g., a static sentinel or class-level discriminator) for pre-persist hashCode to avoid corrupting collections.
For multi-tenant tables, include tenant_id as the leading column of a composite primary key to co-locate tenant data on storage nodes and enforce isolation at the index level.
Never mutate or reuse keys; when a migration renumbers rows, update every referrer and invalidate caches, identity maps and stored links in the same atomic operation.

Document the key generation strategy in the schema and in the code convention: a sequence column, IDENTITY, UUID generator, or hi-lo table — each has different operational properties for backup, replication and sharding.
Expose the identity field through a stable wire format (Relay global IDs, opaque tokens) so client-side caching and server-side storage can agree on the same identifier.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) — Identity Field (Object-Relational Structural Patterns; ch. 12 of the online edition); the pattern's originating catalog.

Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity at the Heart of Software (2003) — Entities: objects defined by a thread of identity rather than attributes; the Aggregate Root pattern enforces identity-based access boundaries.
Krasner, 'Entity Identity vs Database Primary Key', Enterprise Craftsmanship (2018) — precise distinction between domain identity and storage-level primary key.

Vlad Mihalcea, 'How to implement equals and hashCode using the JPA entity identifier', VladMihalcea.com (2016) — definitive treatment of equals/hashCode contract violations for ORM entities with database-generated keys.
Wikipedia, 'Hi/Lo algorithm' — overview of the hi-lo key-generation strategy for pre-allocating identifiers before INSERT.
AWS DynamoDB documentation, 'Optimistic Locking' — version-number-based optimistic concurrency control; the identity field targets the row the version belongs to.

Facebook, 'GraphQL Global Object Identification Specification — Relay' (relay.dev) — globally unique node IDs built from the entity's identity as a base64 type-prefixed string, enabling standardised refetch.
Colin Mackay, 'Composite Primary Key with TenantId', Oracle/Java community — tenant_id as the leading column of a composite primary key for multi-tenant data isolation.
Authgear, 'Time-Sortable Identifiers Explained: UUIDv7, ULID, and Snowflake' (2026) — comparison of time-ordered, application-generated key strategies for distributed systems.
